23fe5a8c-d1c2-4e74-975b-b4b30028ce5d.one_liner: Kansas City Fed's Jeff Schmidt (a 2025 FOMC dissenter) discusses atomic settlement in payments, Fed balance-sheet effects on long rates, an accommodative r-star, and the still-murky reaction function under new Chair Kevin Warsh with inflation stuck in the mid-3s.
23fe5a8c-d1c2-4e74-975b-b4b30028ce5d.recap: Recorded at the 2026 Jackson Hole symposium (themed 'financial innovation in payments'), Odd Lots hosts interview Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmidt. He frames the payments theme around 'atomic settlement' -- instant, simultaneously-reconciled payments moving through the $5-10 trillion/day Fed system -- which he says will raise the importance of duration and liquidity management. On rates, Schmidt notes the Fed only directly controls the short end, though balance-sheet actions post-2008 and post-2020 pulled in duration and influenced longer rates. He attributes the rise in long yields (30-year above 5%) to competition between public and private credit demand, much of it driven by AI/data-center buildout crowding out other industries for commodities like steel, copper and grains. He says the labor market looks solid (unemployment fell to 4.1%) but inflation, which surged into the mid-3s, has not yet been tamed, and he worries about the Fed's credibility if it isn't seen taking inflation seriously -- consistent with his dissents last year as a voting member favoring tighter policy. He views r-star as normalizing but likely structurally higher than pre-2008, judging current policy fairly accommodative. On new Chair Warsh, Schmidt praises his openness to internal debate ('good family fight') but acknowledges Warsh's reaction function remains unclear, with newly formed Fed task forces (data, communications) not yet in dialogue with regional presidents -- that engagement is expected only once their research is published.
terms: FOMC -- Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's monetary policy-setting body
r-star -- the theoretical neutral real interest rate consistent with stable inflation and full employment

3655ef36-a18c-11f1-aeca-cbd655fc898d.one_liner: Deep dive on Treasury's TGA-funded bond buybacks, RRP-to-zero, and a Fed-chair dilemma between hawkish long-end/dovish front-end policy going into Jackson Hole -- core money-market and rates plumbing for a repo desk, wrapped around a Druckenmiller op-ed spat and a long AI/crypto-bubble tangent.
3655ef36-a18c-11f1-aeca-cbd655fc898d.recap: Hosts on Blockworks' Forward Guidance Roundup open by noting markets are range-bound into Labor Day, with policymakers actively suppressing volatility (oil, yields) ahead of Jackson Hole. The main story is Stan Druckenmiller's op-ed (reportedly AI-assisted) criticizing Treasury Secretary Bessent's use of bond buybacks to cap long-end yields, arguing the 30-year is the last fiscal disciplinarian and that any 'crisis' at 5.5% yields is really 'an invoice' for Congress, not something Treasury should paper over. The hosts debate whether this signals a rift among Soros-lineage officials (Bessent, Fed Chair Warsh) or is a coordinated trial balloon shifting blame to Congress. They then discuss a CNBC leak that Treasury could tap its ~$1tn TGA balance to fund expanded bond purchases, noting this is largely a timing trick versus issuing more bills, but signals Bessent's intent to fight yields above 5% aggressively. Looking ahead to Warsh's Jackson Hole speech, they lay out two scenarios: talking hawkish on the long end/balance sheet while staying dovish on the front end (rates, possibly reviving reserve purchases to manage bill-driven SOFR basis stress), versus talking tough with no real teeth since a rate hike isn't on the table. They conclude the setup is a 'nothing burger' for yields short-term but structurally bearish long-term, with the recent selloff driven mainly by term premium rather than rate expectations. The episode closes with a long tangent comparing Anthropic's rumored IPO/valuation hype to the 2021 crypto L1 bubble, and reaffirming a preference for gold/Bitcoin 'debasement trades' over bonds.
terms: TGA -- Treasury General Account, the US Treasury's main operating cash account held at the Federal Reserve
RRP -- overnight reverse repurchase facility at the Federal Reserve
SOFR -- Secured Overnight Financing Rate, the primary US overnight repo-based reference rate

4f8e48be-58f1-4103-a9bd-b4b30134770d.implications: For a credit/repo desk, the key signals are: hyperscaler/NVIDIA-linked IG issuance keeps growing and could pressure tech/IG spreads if capex guidance ever turns down; NVIDIA's growing off-balance-sheet backstops and SPV-based data-center financing (private credit, structured with amortizing tranches) are a structured-credit exposure worth monitoring for contingent-liability build-up; and neocloud names (CoreWeave, Nebius) are flagged as the most levered, capital-markets-dependent links in the chain and the likely first stress point.
key_claims: Hyperscaler/AI capex is roughly $800bn this year and expected to reach at least $1tn next year (Goldberg)

4f8e48be-58f1-4103-a9bd-b4b30134770d.one_liner: A semis equity analyst and a credit analyst debate whether record hyperscaler/AI debt issuance and NVIDIA's vendor-financing backstops are prudent balance-sheet use or an early-stage credit bubble, directly bearing on IG issuance, SPV structuring, and off-balance-sheet risk.
4f8e48be-58f1-4103-a9bd-b4b30134770d.recap: Bloomberg's Credit Edge hosts Jay Goldberg (Seaport Research, semis equity) alongside BI credit analyst Rob Schiffman to debate AI-driven debt issuance. Hyperscaler capex is running near $800bn this year, headed toward $1tn+ next year, funded increasingly by record bond issuance and private-credit platforms (NVIDIA's $500bn financing platform with major financial/real-estate institutions). Goldberg argues we're approaching, but not yet at, true 'circular financing' -- NVIDIA is 'enabling' rather than manufacturing demand, but its backstops (roughly $30bn in disclosed CoreWeave/Nebius guarantees, likely growing) plus supply-chain and startup commitments create contingent liabilities that sit in footnotes, not the balance sheet. He worries these backstops will be called just as NVIDIA's own cash flow softens. Schiffman counters that Moody's just affirmed NVIDIA Aa1 with positive outlook including off-balance-sheet items, that third-party private credit/equity capital (not NVIDIA) is funding much of the platform, and that SPV/off-balance-sheet structuring reflects cash-flow matching (amortizing 15-20yr debt vs 30yr) rather than debt-hiding, since rating agencies add it all back anyway. They discuss GPU residual value/obsolescence (2-year paybacks, stable-to-rising secondary prices), concentration risk (7 companies, two FCF-negative, driving all AI capex), circularity in cloud-compute credits between hyperscalers and OpenAI/Anthropic, and neoclouds (CoreWeave, Nebius) as the likely first crack point if capex growth stalls. Both expect the AI buildout to continue but see rising odds of casualties, likening the setup to 2007-era leverage build-up rather than the dot-com bubble.
terms: SPV -- special purpose vehicle, a legally separate entity used to isolate project assets/cash flows and debt, often kept off the sponsor's balance sheet
CUDA -- NVIDIA's proprietary software/programming platform for its GPUs, a key competitive moat
TPU -- Tensor Processing Unit, Google's custom AI accelerator chip

b324a08e-dea3-42b2-813d-fec5b475d2bb.one_liner: A Guggenheim-linked $1.18bn loan trading at distressed 73 cents exposes how Mark Walter's TWG insurers (Delaware Life, Clear Spring) mislabeled $20bn+ of affiliated private-credit loans, raising fresh doubts about valuation integrity across the insurance-backed private credit complex.
b324a08e-dea3-42b2-813d-fec5b475d2bb.recap: The episode examines a distressed-priced loan tied to Guggenheim Partners CEO Mark Walter's broader business network, which spans asset management (Guggenheim Investments), a holding company (TWG Global), and two life insurers, Delaware Life and Clear Spring. A $1.18bn first-lien loan due 2031, issued at par in November 2024, has fallen to roughly 72.5-73 cents despite no missed payments, a level the host frames as market-implied distress. The decline followed a 38% revenue drop and 77% earnings collapse at Guggenheim Investments, partly blamed on delayed advisory-fee recognition at Guggenheim Private Investments, itself the subject of a whistleblower complaint. Separately, Delaware Life and Clear Spring disclosed that over $20bn of investments should have been classified as "affiliated" but weren't, following federal grand jury subpoenas and an SEC inquiry. The host argues this reflects a broader pattern: insurers' long-duration annuity premiums are used as cheap, sticky leverage that private-credit sponsors funnel into related-party loans, warehouse facilities, CLOs, and even trophy assets (Dodgers, the since-sold Lakers stake), while risk sits with policyholders. S&P cut Delaware Life's outlook to negative; the insurers plan to shed roughly $6.5bn of affiliated exposure. The host connects this to wider private-credit opacity — BDCs trading below NAV, rising redemptions in non-traded credit funds — and argues fragmented state/federal regulatory oversight means no one has a full picture of affiliate chains, making the Walter case a potential template for scrutinizing similar insurer-sponsor structures industry-wide.
terms: BDC -- Business Development Company, a publicly traded closed-end fund that lends to and invests in private/middle-market companies
CLO -- Collateralized Loan Obligation, a securitization backed by a pool of leveraged loans
First lien loan -- a secured loan with the highest priority claim on pledged collateral in a default
